review.headline: Your design passes all tests, survives key failures and keeps headroom at peak.

items.text: You survived a server dying at peak, the primary failing and a cold cache restart. That is the core of this brief, because fresh links must not be lost and opens must keep working.
items.ask: Walk me through what happens to a new link when a machine dies.

items.text: You also passed the evening peak and the quiet afternoon, with 31 % spare on your tightest promise, the budget. Peak opens stay comfortable without breaking the monthly limit.
items.ask: Why is budget your tightest promise, and what would you trim first if costs rose?

items.text: Steady behaviour in both quiet and peak periods gives you clear evidence for capacity talk. You can point to the same design holding across very different customer demand.

next.text: Use this as your base design. Now practise explaining failure handling and cost choices out loud, in that order.

review.headline: Your design passes a quiet afternoon but collapses in the evening peak.

items.text: Your api tier receives 2,525 calls a second in the evening peak but can serve at most 500 calls a second. That overload alone explains the failed peak test and the slow responses.
items.ask: How would you spread peak opens across more capacity within budget?

items.text: GET_LINK took 472.7 ms at the 99th percentile; the promise is 100 ms. Slowest hop: api at 505 % of capacity.
Your api has no spare. If it fails, both GET_LINK and CREATE_LINK stop, so one failure takes down the whole service.
items.ask: What happens to creates and opens if your single api tier fails?

items.text: Your design passes a quiet afternoon with 54 % to spare on its tightest promise. The basic path works, so the challenge is peak headroom rather than the core approach.

next.text: Relieve the api tier under peak opens first, by adding capacity or by serving more reads away from it. Then recheck cost and latency at peak.

review.headline: Your design is too slow at the evening peak because reads are bottlenecked by the database.

items.text: Your evening peak promise is p99 ≤ 100 ms but you reach p99 126.9 ms. The database is the slowest hop and runs at 86 % at that moment. That is why the peak fails.
items.ask: Why does your read path hit the database on every open at peak?

items.text: Your database load swings from 7 % in quiet times to 86 % at peak. You have very little headroom left. Any small rise in opens will push latency higher.
items.ask: What happens to latency when load grows a little beyond peak?

items.text: Your quiet afternoon test passes with 34 % to spare on its tightest promise. The basic shape works when load is low. The weakness only appears as load rises.

next.text: Focus on the database part first. Work on the repair for that part and recheck its peak load at 86 % before you change anything else.

review.headline: Your reads and cost pass, but acknowledged links are lost when the database primary fails.

items.text: Your acknowledged writes are lost when the database primary fails. That breaks the core promise that a just created link is never lost. You need durability for CREATE_LINK before anything else.
items.ask: How would you make sure a write is acknowledged only after it survives a primary failure?

items.text: You pass the evening peak with headroom. The busiest part is the api tier at 63 %, while {{path:GET_LINK.p99}} for the read path stays comfortable. That shows your read scaling is sound under SMS load.
items.ask: Where would you add capacity first if peak traffic doubled?

items.text: You survive a server dying at peak and fit the budget with 31 % to spare. Cost is not your problem here. Focus on durability rather than trimming parts.

next.text: Make the database wait for its replicas before acknowledging a create, then recheck the primary failure case.

review.headline: Your design fails because repeated short codes break its core promise.

items.text: Your random codes do not guarantee uniqueness at scale. The judge found about 11,64,153 repeats expected when it expected no repeated ids. A code must never point at two URLs.
items.ask: How would you guarantee a code is never reused across all creators?

items.text: Correctness failed outright in the quiet afternoon test, with 0 of 5 tests passed. Performance and cost cannot rescue a design that repeats ids. Fix uniqueness before anything else.

next.text: Add more bits to the ids part, following the suggested repair direction, and recheck uniqueness before anything else.

review.headline: Your cache keeps edited links far too stale to pass.

items.text: Your GET_LINK path can serve a URL long after it has been edited. The cache holds data up to 86400 s old old, while the limit is at most 3600 s old. That breaks the freshness promise.
items.ask: How will you make a write reach the cache soon enough?

items.text: The design fails the quiet afternoon test and the overall verdict stays wrong. It allows data up to 86400 s old old, against at most 3600 s old. Until freshness is fixed, it will keep failing.
items.ask: What would you change first to bring the age within the limit?

next.text: Clear the cache when the data changes, so reads stop serving the old URL past the allowed limit.

review.headline: Your design is over budget and the database drives most of the cost.

items.text: Your design is over budget. It costs ₹1,43,000 a month against a budget of ₹1,00,000. No test passed, so cost is the first fix. Shrink the part that drives the bill before you tune anything else.

items.text: The database is the main problem. It costs ₹90,000 a month, which is 63 % of the total, while the app tier costs ₹48,000. A smaller database is the obvious place to cut.

review.headline: Your design is unreadable because neither the read path nor the write path reaches any storage.

items.text: Your read path is disconnected. GET_LINK never reaches sql, nosql or objectstore, so an opened code has nowhere to find its long URL. The judge reports 2 unreadable elements in this design.
items.ask: Where should GET_LINK go to fetch the long URL for a code?

items.text: Your write path is also disconnected. CREATE_LINK is never saved because its route does not reach sql, nosql or objectstore. Without a saved mapping a new code cannot be reopened later.
items.ask: Where should CREATE_LINK save the new mapping so it is never lost?

next.text: Reconnect both paths first. Point GET_LINK and CREATE_LINK at the store that holds the code to URL mapping, then explain how you split reads and writes for scale.

review.headline: Your design passed all tests and kept 24 % spare on its tightest promise.

items.text: Your design passed every test. The tightest promise is GET_PASTE latency during an incident, and it still has 24 % to spare. That headroom shows the read path holds under a burst.
items.ask: What would you watch first if incident traffic doubled?

items.text: You also passed the failure tests for a server dying, the database primary failing and the cache restarting. That shows your design does not depend on one healthy part at runtime.
items.ask: Which failure worries you most and how would you prove recovery?

items.text: In a quiet hour you kept 24 % to spare on the tightest promise. You also sit under budget with 24 % to spare. Simpler traffic therefore leaves room, while your incident case uses that room when it matters.
items.ask: Where would you spend any remaining budget, and why there?
